content: The protective efficacy of an intervention is calculated as (1 hazard ratio). In a primary study, the baseline or comparator group was established, and the risk of bias, inconsistency, and indirectness were deemed not serious. However, imprecision was considered serious due to the limited number of events and a wide confidence interval, leading to a one-level downgrade. No significant publication bias was identified. Children aged 5 to 17 months were randomly assigned to receive sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine and amodiaquine (chemoprevention-only group), RTS,S/AS01E (vaccine-only group), or a combination of chemoprevention and RTS,S/AS01E (combination group). In another primary study, the imprecision was rated as very serious due to few events and a very large confidence interval that included the possibility of both benefit and harm, resulting in a two-level downgrade. No serious issues with bias, inconsistency, or indirectness were noted. In a four-dose group, children received three doses of RTS,S/AS01 at months 0, 1, and 2, followed by a booster dose at month 20. The control group received a comparator vaccine at the same intervals. Protective efficacy was calculated as (1 hazard ratio). The study showed no serious risk of bias, inconsistency, or indirectness, but imprecision was serious due to few events and a large confidence interval. A pilot implementation study using cluster-randomized control methodology analyzed 27,678 hospital admissions in children aged 1 to 59 months across three countries from vaccine introduction until April 30, 2021. Among these, 4,853 admissions were vaccine-eligible in implementing areas, compared to 5,141 in comparison areas. Severe malaria accounted for 19% of admissions in comparison areas among children eligible for three doses of the malaria vaccine. No evidence suggested that the introduction of the malaria vaccine increased hospital admissions for meningitis or cerebral malaria. Routine malaria testing was conducted for patients admitted to sentinel hospitals, with results available for 88% of the 27,678 patients. Among children eligible for three vaccine doses, 2,630 tested positive for malaria, with 1,075 cases from implementing areas and 1,555 from comparison areas. No serious risk of bias, inconsistency, or indirectness was identified, but imprecision was serious due to large confidence intervals. In a study of all-cause mortality, children receiving three or four doses of RTS,S/AS01 were compared to a control group. Among girls, the four-dose group had 35 deaths (9 from malaria) out of 1,467 participants, while the control group had 17 deaths (4 from malaria) out of 1,503 participants. Among boys, the four-dose group had 26 deaths (4 from malaria) out of 1,509 participants, compared to 29 deaths (8 from malaria) in the control group. Imprecision was rated as very serious due to few events and wide confidence intervals. In another analysis, 13,682 deaths among children aged 1 to 59 months were reported via community-based mortality surveillance across three countries from April 2019 to March 2021. Excluding deaths due to injury, 2,864 deaths were reported among children eligible for three vaccine doses, with 1,421 from implementing regions and 1,443 from comparison regions. No evidence suggested that the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine introduction affected all-cause mortality differently between girls and boys. Overall, the studies demonstrated no significant increase in hospital admissions for meningitis or cerebral malaria following the introduction of the malaria vaccine. The findings were consistent across various analyses, with no serious issues of bias, inconsistency, or indirectness, although imprecision was frequently noted due to limited events and wide confidence intervals.
